summary: Standardizes the media types application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity, and application/xml-dtd, and defines text/xml variants as aliases. It also standardizes the +xml suffix. It obsoletes RFC 3023 and updates RFC 6839.

eli5.summary: This explains the labels that tell a computer a file is XML, plus the plus-xml ending for related file kinds.

questions: what does +xml media type suffix mean
which encoding wins bom or charset
subtitle: Which MIME type labels an XML document, how its character encoding is decided, and what the +xml suffix means.

tldr.problem: XML can travel inside MIME and HTTP, but MIME labels and XML's own encoding declarations can disagree, and many new formats are built on XML with no common naming convention.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7303 registers application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd, treats the text/ variants as aliases, sets the priority of encoding information (a BOM first, then the charset parameter), and standardizes the +xml suffix.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3023 and updates RFC 6839. UTF-8 without a BOM is recommended, and generic XML tools can recognize any media type ending in +xml.

today: RFC 7303 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3023 and updates RFC 6839. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Three Types, Two Aliases and a Suffix
sections.content:
To let XML network entities be exchanged, RFC 7303 standardizes three media types: application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd. It also defines two aliases, text/xml and text/xml-external-parsed-entity, and a naming convention, the +xml suffix, for other XML-based media types.

XML has been used as the foundation for many other media types, so a shared suffix lets generic tools such as browsers, editors and search engines work with all of them. This RFC replaces RFC 3023. The major differences are aligning the text/ types with the application/ types, adding XPointer fragment identifiers and XML Base, integrating the XPointer registry and updating references.
sections.eli5: There are a few official labels for XML files, plus a rule that any new XML-based label should end in +xml, so programs can spot them.

sections.title: Terms: Entities, Charsets and Encodings
sections.content:
MIME and XML both use the word entity with different meanings. The RFC defines an XML MIME entity as an XML entity encapsulated in a MIME entity, and writes "XML-entity" when it means the XML sense.

It also fixes some vocabulary. A charset parameter is what the MIME Content-Type header declares, and an encoding declaration is what the XML document declares. The actual encoding is the one really used. UTF-8 has only one serialization, labelled utf-8. UTF-16 can be big-endian or little-endian. UTF-32 use is NOT RECOMMENDED for XML MIME entities.
sections.eli5: Two clubs use the same word to mean different things, so this part says which meaning it will use. It also explains the different ways to write down letters in bytes.

sections.title: Deciding the Character Encoding
sections.content:
Up to three sources can describe an entity's encoding: the charset parameter, a byte order mark (BOM) and the XML encoding declaration. The RFC says UTF-8 without a BOM is RECOMMENDED for all XML MIME entities.

For consumers, the priority is simple. A BOM is authoritative if present. Without a BOM, the charset parameter is authoritative if present. When the charset is omitted, XML-aware consumers MUST follow Section 4.3.3 of the XML specification, and XML-unaware consumers SHOULD NOT assume a default encoding.

For producers, XML-unaware software MUST NOT supply a charset parameter unless the encoding is reliably known. The RFC singles out web servers configured with a default charset as likely to violate this. XML-aware producers SHOULD supply a charset and/or BOM for non-UTF-8 entities lacking an encoding declaration, and SHOULD remove or correct a declaration known to be wrong, for example after transcoding.

BOM handling during conversion is spelled out. Converting UTF-16 to a non-UTF-8 encoding MUST strip the BOM. Entities labelled utf-16le or utf-16be MUST NOT begin with a BOM.
sections.eli5: If a file has a sticker on the cover and a note inside saying different things, this tells you which to trust: the special mark at the very start first, then the sticker on the outside.

sections.title: Which Type for Which XML Entity
sections.content:
XML has four kinds of entity that can travel in MIME, and each has a recommended type.

  • Document entities: application/xml or text/xml, or a more specific type, SHOULD be used.
  • External DTD subsets and external parameter entities: application/xml-dtd SHOULD be used, and application/xml and text/xml MUST NOT be used.
  • External parsed entities: application/xml-external-parsed-entity or the text/ alias SHOULD be used. The generic XML types MUST NOT be used unless the entity is also a well-formed document entity.

RFC 3023 had treated text/xml differently for character encoding. This RFC aligns the text/ types with the application/ types, but application/xml and application/xml-external-parsed-entity are still RECOMMENDED to avoid confusion with the earlier distinction.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of XML pieces each get a different label. A whole document, a rulebook for documents and a loose snippet each have their own sticker.

sections.title: The +xml Suffix
sections.content:
When a new media type is introduced for an XML-based format, its name SHOULD end with +xml unless generic XML processing is in some way inappropriate. Applications can then check the last four characters of the subtype to learn that the content is XML. Only subtypes that really represent XML MIME entities may register with this suffix. The change controller for the suffix registration became the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).

Such types SHOULD define the charset parameter, though it may be omitted for types restricted to UTF-8 or to UTF-8 and UTF-16. Types that do not use +xml SHOULD say their charset parameter and encoding considerations are the same as application/xml, and SHOULD carry over this RFC's security considerations.

An Accept header such as */*+xml is not allowed and will not match only +xml types.

Fragment identifiers follow the XPointer framework. Conforming applications MUST support the element scheme, and the xml:base attribute may be used to embed a base URI.
sections.eli5: If your new label is for a kind of XML, end its name with +xml. Then any XML-reading program knows it can at least open the file.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XML MIME entities are parsed and processed by the recipient, and an application that executes arbitrary command strings found inside them may be at risk. Anything stored outside the user's direct control, such as style sheets, XSL transformations, XML-entity declarations and DTDs, can be a source of insecurity, so a document's security depends on everything it recursively references.

The RFC describes several attacks. Edited DTDs can break validation or redefine default attribute values. XML-entity spoofing can insert text where an entity reference is used. Display escape sequences can lock a keyboard or reprogram keys, so display processors SHOULD filter such material or reset their settings. Nested but non-recursive entity expansions can exhaust a computer's finite resources, for example when XML-entity A consists of 100 copies of B, which consists of 100 copies of C, and so on.
sections.eli5: An XML file can point to other files, and if someone sneaks bad changes into those, your file changes too. Programs should be careful about what they follow and how much they unpack.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3023
sections.content: Appendix D summarizes the major differences from RFC 3023. XPointer was added as the fragment identifier syntax for all the XML media types, and XML Base was added as a way to specify base URIs. The language about character sets was updated to match the W3C TAG finding on media type registration. A BOM now takes priority if present. Many references were updated, the existence of XML 1.1 was acknowledged, and justifications that were appropriate when XML was new were removed, including the whole of the original Appendix A.
sections.eli5: This lists what is different from the old rulebook: new ways to point inside a file, a clearer order for deciding the alphabet, and tidier explanations.
